title: Diagnose the Performance Problem Before Prescribing the Cure
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that leaders' first explanation for a team member's poor performance is often wrong, because they blame the person too heavily and underweight causes outside the person. It lists more than two dozen possible causes, from unclear expectations to strain at home, and cites Gallup data showing that many workers lack clear expectations or adequate tools. The recommended approach gives the team member an ownership role in the diagnosis, starting with specific facts and an open question about what is in the way. The author then asks leaders to judge whether the root cause is addressable at all, since motivation, self-discipline and anxiety are seldom fixable by a leader. For addressable causes, short performance experiments are offered as a gentler and often equally effective alternative to performance improvement plans. A failed experiment is treated as new information that sends the pair back to the diagnosis, and a respectful role change or exit is the honest conclusion only after fair testing.
points: First reads on poor performance are often inaccurate because leaders place more blame on the person and less on situational factors.
Gallup data that only half of workers know what is expected of them suggests many performance gaps originate in the system, not the individual.
Leaders should invite the team member into the diagnosis, laying out facts and asking what is getting in the way before offering a view.
Some root causes, such as low motivation or anxiety, are seldom fixable by a leader, so honest triage of what can change comes before any intervention.
A short, targeted performance experiment is a lighter alternative to a PIP, and a failed one becomes information for the next attempt rather than a verdict.
quotes: Unfortunately, research consistently shows that many leaders’ first read on poor performance is often inaccurate. Leaders commonly place more blame on the team member and less on other factors that can influence performance.

Gallup finds that only half of team members worldwide clearly know what is expected of them, and only a third say they have the tools to do their work effectively. Many of the likely causes sit outside the person.
Good leaders don’t rush to a judgment about why a team member is performing poorly. Instead, they give the team member an ownership role in the diagnosis.
They lay out the gap with specific facts and examples and ask what is getting in the way before offering their own view.
While performance improvement plans (PIPs) are a popular choice for encouraging change, performance experiments are less drastic and often just as effective.

When an experiment fails to close the gap, good leaders treat the result as new information rather than a verdict. They return to the diagnosis with the team member and ask what the experiment revealed.
What matters most is that the leader reaches that decision through careful diagnosis, fair testing, and collaboration with the team member.
